# The Architecture 2.0 Reviewer's Checklist {#sec-appendix-a-reviewer-checklist}

A reviewer judging a paper, an artifact package, or a design report on AI for computer architecture needs to establish that the reported advance is genuine progress in the architecture rather than an artifact of the comparison. The order of inspection matters. Problem formulation and baseline fairness come first, because a flaw at the starting line undermines every conclusion drawn from downstream measurements; representations, data hygiene, proxy fidelity, and workflow execution follow.

Hardware raises the stakes of that inspection because it answers to physical and formal ground truth. Software can often be patched in the field, whereas a logic bug in silicon can force a mask respin and cost a market window, and a model that reaches low loss on an abstract dataset can still fail when its output has to close timing, stay within a power budget, and pass design rules. Because architecture studies span many abstraction levels, the evidence one paper owes differs from the evidence another owes. Demanding tapeout signoff from a microarchitectural policy study is unreasonable, yet accepting unsynthesized, unlinted register-transfer level (RTL) from a paper that claims implementation-ready hardware leaves no evidence that the design can actually be built. Rather than maintaining separate rubrics for each abstraction level, the checklist handles this range through its recording labels: any item that falls outside a paper's claim is marked not applicable, and a reviewer should expect to mark several.

One checklist serves three readers: a reviewer evaluating a submission item by item, an author checking before submission what evidence the work will need to supply, and a student learning what the field counts as evidence and why. Each item states the core question, the failure mode that makes the question necessary, and what credible evidence looks like, closing with a one-line summary of what the check catches. Because none of the items depends on the specialized terms or record formats introduced earlier in this book, a program committee or design team can use the checklist on its own.

The seventeen checks are grouped into five areas that follow the order of inspection, from problem framing down to workflow execution and signoff ownership. Cross-references in this list are for readers of this book and are not part of any item.

1. **Area 1: System Framing, Problem Scope, and Method Justification** (is learning warranted; matched baselines; @sec-from-architecture-10-to-architecture-20)
2. **Area 2: Data Representations and Physical Grounding** (hardware semantics, structural faithfulness, legal decodability; @sec-data-representations-world-models)
3. **Area 3: Data Integrity, Leakage, and Generalization Boundaries** (benchmark decontamination, temporal and feature leakage, out-of-distribution transfer; @sec-data-representations-world-models; @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect)
4. **Area 4: Learning Methods and Proxy Fidelity** (validation of generated artifacts at the level the claim requires, tail-ranking correlation, optimizer anti-gaming, multi-objective constraint integrity; @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization)
5. **Area 5: System Orchestration, Reproducibility, and Ownership** (lineage, replayable environments, gross cost accounting, human commitment authority; @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces; @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect; @sec-what-architect-owns)

## Recording Findings

When working through those five areas, record for each applicable item what evidence the work supplies, where that evidence appears, and what it establishes or leaves open. Findings describe the state of the evidence; they do not grade the work. The four labels below provide a compact shorthand, though plain-language notes or an existing review form serve the same purpose.

- **Supported.** The work supplies the evidence the item asks for, and the reviewer can point to where it appears.
- **Conditional.** The evidence satisfies the check only within a stated restriction, such as a single technology node or a single benchmark family. The reviewer records that restriction and notes whether the claim stays within it. A single random seed, for example, documents one run but leaves variability across seeds unresolved; by itself, it does not support a broader reliability claim.
- **Unresolved.** The available evidence does not establish whether the failure mode the item checks for has occurred. Record what is missing alongside what the supplied evidence does establish. Absent information is not evidence of failure; if the work instead demonstrates a failure, describe it directly and state which part of the claim it undermines.
- **Not applicable.** The claim does not reach the item. A microarchitectural policy paper whose claims are bounded to cycle-level simulation does not owe post-layout signoff, and a paper on learned cost models does not owe placement legalization results unless its claims depend on producing legal layouts. Record briefly why the item falls outside the claim.

These item-level labels do not add up to a numerical score. No fixed count of supported items guarantees acceptance, no count of unresolved items forces rejection, and the items carry no weights. Instead, the reviewer states how each restriction or gap bounds the claim, identifies what an unfavorable result would undermine, and forms the overall recommendation as a separate judgment. A submission can supply the evidence for every applicable item and still make a headline claim that its evidence does not reach; conversely, a paper with several conditional or unresolved checks can still be worth publishing once its claim is narrowed to match what was tested.

Item-level findings here also differ from the program-level claim judgments in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect, which assess whether an overall program claim is supported, unsupported, or unresolved through matched comparisons and declared decision boundaries. Every applicable item in this checklist can be satisfied while the overarching program claim remains unresolved because the comparison lacks the resolving power to decide it. Reviews that use both vocabularies should therefore specify whether a finding concerns an individual check or the overall claim.

## Area 1: System Framing, Problem Scope, and Method Justification

With the recording rules in place, the review begins at the system boundary. Before examining model architectures, loss functions, or training curves, a reviewer asks whether the problem formulation is sound and what the proposed method offers over relevant alternatives. Area 1 checks whether learning fits the problem, whether baseline comparisons are fair, what the work contributes beyond an underlying pretrained model, and whether the workflow saves engineering time overall.

- **Check 1.1: The Method Justification and Overkill Test.** Assess whether simpler analytical formulations, dynamic programming, integer linear programming, or greedy heuristics already provide suitable alternatives under the problem's constraints, comparing solution quality, runtime, and any guarantees relevant to the claim. Learned methods bring training overhead, inference latency, nondeterminism, and harder failure interpretation. When a problem has exploitable structure (such as an analytical bound like Roofline [@Williams2009Roofline], optimal substructure suited to dynamic programming, or a scheduling rule suited to a greedy heuristic), the evaluation should explain what classical tools leave unresolved and where learning helps; an upper bound, for instance, need not provide a way to construct a design that reaches it. Conversely, high-dimensional nonlinear interactions, layout parasitics, and multi-objective tradeoffs can motivate a learned approach, but their presence alone does not prove its advantage. The evidence need not show that every classical alternative fails, but it should compare relevant methods on the stated task and account for run-to-run variability [@AgarwalEtAl2021StatisticalPrecipice]. **Catches:** added method complexity whose benefit over a suitable simpler approach has not been established.

- **Check 1.2: Matched Compute Budgets and Baseline Parity.** Once relevant baselines are chosen, verify that learned search (reinforcement learning, Bayesian optimization, or neural tree search) is compared against credible conventional baselines with documented tuning effort and matched resource budgets [@AgarwalEtAl2021StatisticalPrecipice; @ChengEtAl2023MacroPlacement]. When a multi-GPU learned optimizer runs $10^5$ design evaluations while a simulated-annealing or genetic baseline is capped at $10^2$ evaluations on a single CPU core, the reported margin alone cannot separate a better algorithm from a larger compute budget. Match the budget that governs the claim: sample limits for evaluation efficiency, wall-clock time for turnaround, or simulator and license invocations when tool capacity constrains the work. A single comparison does not have to equalize all three budgets at once. Plotting quality-of-results curves against the governing budgets, with hardware and tuning effort disclosed, lets readers see where an advantage holds. Include training and preparation costs in that accounting, and state any assumptions about amortizing them across later searches. **Catches:** a resource advantage presented as evidence of algorithmic superiority.

- **Check 1.3: Methodological Contribution and Model Dependence.** Alongside external baselines, identify what the work contributes beyond the underlying model and test whether that contribution explains the reported improvement. Contributions may include decoding guided by an abstract syntax tree (AST), neurosymbolic grammar verification, closed-loop compiler repair, a domain representation, a specialized training objective, or a prompt-based harness; VeriGen, for example, evaluates a model fine-tuned specifically for Verilog generation [@ThakurEtAl2023VeriGen]. A prompt template wrapped around a commercial foundation model requires the same scrutiny: what does it add over direct prompting, under what conditions does it help, and how sensitive is the result to model and prompt choices? A prompt-centric workflow should compare against simpler prompts and test sensitivity to sampling temperature, random seed, and prompt wording. Where the claim extends across checkpoints or model families, test that scope; otherwise, state the dependence on the evaluated model. Judge prompt choices by their measurable effects on correctness, quality, cost, and repeatability rather than by stylistic preference. **Catches:** improvement attributed to the proposed method without evidence separating its contribution from the underlying model's capability.

- **Check 1.4: End-to-End Workflow Speedup and Amdahl's Law.** Finally, audit total human engineering effort and elapsed time across the workflow rather than timing the automated step in isolation. Amdahl's law explains why accelerating one stage yields a smaller overall speedup when other stages remain unchanged [@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor; @AltafWood2017LogCA]. In hardware design, automation can also expand the work in those downstream stages: if a tool drafts an accelerator block in seconds instead of days but introduces timing bugs and protocol glitches that take weeks of extra manual triage and formal verification to fix, project throughput can fall (@sec-data-scarcity-verification-load). When a paper claims workflow speedup, it should compare paths that reach the same verification standard, reporting human interaction time, prompt iteration counts, and manual repair edits alongside generation time. A workflow can still achieve net acceleration even when downstream verification and debugging grow, provided savings elsewhere outweigh that growth, but human effort should be reported separately from elapsed wall-clock time so that parallel execution or unattended tool runs do not obscure the tradeoff. **Catches:** a local speedup presented as a workflow improvement without accounting for added work elsewhere.

## Area 2: Data Representations and Physical Grounding

Once the problem framing and baseline comparisons are clear, the review turns to how circuits, layouts, and traces are encoded for the model. Learned methods operate on representations rather than on silicon directly. To support an architectural claim, a representation must retain the structural and physical properties that govern the claim, and those properties must survive translation through the relevant compilation and implementation steps. Area 2 checks structural faithfulness, legal decodability, placement legalization, and consistency across abstraction levels. As throughout the checklist, the required checks follow what the study claims: not every representation must encode every physical detail, and not every study requires physical signoff.

- **Check 2.1: Hardware Semantic and Structural Faithfulness.** Verify that the representation preserves the circuit properties relevant to the claim, such as module hierarchy, multi-clock domains, bitwidths, control and data flow, and spatial adjacency. Because circuits are spatial, concurrent, and hierarchical [@BachrachEtAl2012Chisel], the review should inspect whether flattening a netlist or tokenizing source code discards information needed for the task. A flat token sequence is not by itself evidence of semantic loss, so long as the sequence encodes what the model and downstream tools must recover (@sec-hardware-representation-formats). When a study makes a claim about wire congestion, layout parasitics, or modularity, the evaluation should state which spatial or structural relationships the encoding retains and show how the workflow uses them. Where the workflow generates new designs, it should also include decoded examples and verify that port interfaces, signal widths, and relevant constraints survive conversion into the files consumed by downstream tools. **Catches:** a representation that cannot express the property the claim is about.

- **Check 2.2: Legalization Robustness and Post-Legalization Quality Delta.** When a continuous generative model (such as a diffusion model or a variational autoencoder) proposes floorplans or macro placements, check whether automated placement tools can legalize the geometry and require disclosure of any manual intervention [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement; @ChengEtAl2026UpdatedAssessment]. Floating-point coordinate predictions often leave macros overlapping, violate cell-density limits, or create pin blockages that obstruct routing. When legalization shifts macros to resolve those violations, the wirelength and timing predicted for the raw proposal may no longer describe the resulting layout. The evaluation should therefore report the automated legalization success rate alongside quality of results measured both before and after legalization, distinguishing fast surrogate estimates from measurements taken by downstream implementation tools. Passing placement legalization alone does not establish design-rule checking (DRC) or layout-versus-schematic (LVS) success; report those checks separately when the claim reaches manufacturable layout, and otherwise state what remains untested. **Catches:** placement quality measured before the placement was legal, or legalization presented as physical signoff.

- **Check 2.3: Multi-Fidelity Representation Consistency.** Just as continuous coordinates can shift during legalization, conclusions drawn from a high-level abstraction (such as a transaction-level model or an instruction trace) can shift when evaluated at a lower level. High-level models routinely omit or simplify resource contention, cache port conflicts, and wire parasitics [@AkramSawalha2019SimulatorSurvey]. Because a search algorithm will favor candidates that benefit from those omissions, a Pareto frontier found in a fast search model requires lower-level validation before it can support an implementation claim. Whenever conclusions are meant to hold at a lower level, the evaluation should compare representative designs, including the selected candidates, at the fidelity the conclusion requires, whether through cycle-accurate RTL simulation, post-synthesis timing analysis, or physical implementation. Report whether candidate rankings and claimed tradeoffs survive and explain any reversals that change which design wins, since positive correlation across the whole space can still hide an error in the chosen candidate. Any conclusion without lower-level evaluation must be bounded to the abstraction actually tested. **Catches:** a ranking that reverses at the abstraction level needed to support the claim.

## Area 3: Data Integrity, Leakage, and Generalization Boundaries

Even a faithful representation can yield misleading results if evaluation circuits appeared in training, test information enters the feature pipeline, or predictions extend beyond the conditions evaluated. Area 3 checks what the dataset and split structure actually support: performance on familiar designs, generalization to held-out designs, or transfer to a changed architecture problem. As before, the required isolation depends on the scope of the claim.

- **Check 3.1: Benchmark Decontamination, Zero-Point Baselines, and Harness Isolation.** Examine whether an autoregressive model could have encountered the public benchmark suites used to evaluate it, such as VerilogEval [@VerilogEval] or ChiPBench [@WangEtAl2025ChiPBench], and whether a tool-using evaluation harness isolates state between independent episodes and rejects vacuous passes [@ZhuEtAl2025AgenticBenchmarks]. Residual files or memory state leaking across episodes, or reward rubrics that credit an empty response or a reset-only module, can inflate reported capability without solving the hardware task. The benchmark diagnostics in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect separate harness-exploit scores from contamination indicators; the latter flag suspect overlap but do not establish how much memorization contributed to performance (@fig-benchmark-health-zero-point-contamination). Authors should report what is known about training-data overlap, which contamination checks were run, and what remains unknown; where pretraining corpora are undisclosed, failing to detect overlap does not prove the benchmark was unseen. If canary strings are used, explain their role and what their detection or absence shows. Document which filesystem and memory state is cleared between independent episodes and which resources remain intentionally shared. Finally, run a do-nothing baseline (an empty module or no-op generator) to establish the zero-point floor, and test parameterized mutants that break textbook patterns, such as a non-power-of-two first-in, first-out (FIFO) depth, an inverted handshake polarity, or a custom instruction-set extension. Such variants probe behavior beyond verbatim templates, though passing them does not by itself prove that the original benchmark is uncontaminated. **Catches:** possible test-set recall, unintended cross-episode state, and credit awarded for doing nothing.

- **Check 3.2: Temporal, Hierarchical, and Feature Leakage.** Beyond external benchmark overlap, check that the study's training, validation, and test partitions match its generalization claim. Holding out leaf design blocks tests a different boundary from holding out system families or later tapeout revisions; a study need not impose all three boundaries unless its claims require them. Computing normalization statistics over the full dataset before splitting, or partitioning randomly across interconnected submodules of the same chip, exposes test information during training and undermines a claim of independent evaluation [@BaggerlyCoombes2009; @Balloccu2024Leakage]. Similarly, placement hints or post-synthesis timing from a later tapeout must not be visible to a model predicting an earlier stage. The feature pipeline should state when each input becomes available in the design flow, confirm which data are used to fit normalization and preprocessing, and disclose whether shared subcircuits or related revisions appear on both sides of a split, explaining whether that overlap reflects intended design reuse or compromises the holdout boundary. **Catches:** test information entering through preprocessing, shared subcircuits, or features unavailable at prediction time.

- **Check 3.3: Out-of-Distribution Validity Envelopes.** Even with clean data splits, a surrogate is only tested within the regime covered by its evaluation set. Require an explicit statement of those evaluated conditions, including the process design kit (PDK), microarchitectural topology, and circuit scale. Moving from planar SkyWater SKY130 at $130\ \text{nm}$ to a FinFET node, or from fixed 2D aspect ratios to a 3D chiplet arrangement, changes the prediction task and calls for new evidence. Although distributional shift is a general learned-system risk [@AmodeiEtAl2016Concrete] whose presence alone does not prove that a hardware model will fail, a study claiming transfer across regimes must check which device, interconnect, and geometric assumptions change and test predictions against target-condition results (@sec-support-limits). Physics-informed constraints (such as RC scaling and IR-drop equations) and uncertainty estimates can help flag implausible or unsupported predictions, provided those mechanisms are themselves checked under the target conditions and any unverified regime is stated as outside the evaluated range. **Catches:** an extrapolation presented with more confidence than the target-condition evidence supports.

## Area 4: Learning Methods and Proxy Fidelity

Once representation and data hygiene are established, the review turns to how generative synthesizers, predictive surrogates, and closed-loop optimizers support the reported claims, whether those method families are used alone or together. Fast proxies inevitably simplify the hardware behavior they approximate, and active search systematically favors candidates where proxy error looks like a design gain. Area 4 therefore checks artifact verification, surrogate accuracy on selected candidates, simulator blind spots, and multi-objective constraint accounting against what the study claims to establish.

- **Check 4.1: Generative Synthesis Beyond Compilation and Pass@1.** Audit generated RTL for the functional and stateful behavior required by the claim rather than stopping at compilation or shallow testbench passes [@ThakurEtAl2023VeriGen; @VerilogEval]. Because `Pass@1` measures single-sample success under whatever testbench the benchmark provides, a high `Pass@1` on combinational leaf modules (such as multiplexers or shift registers) does not establish correctness for complex multicycle logic. In stateful hardware, common failure modes include functional vacuity [@BeerEtAl2001Vacuity], clock-domain-crossing metastability, asynchronous reset glitches, and unintended inferred latches. Depending on the design and claim, appropriate evidence may include lint checks (`verilator --lint-only -Wall`), inspection of inferred storage elements, clock-domain crossing (CDC) analysis, nonvacuous formal proofs with SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA), bounded model checking with stated bounds, and logic synthesis, while an open PDK and open tools make physical implementation checks accessible [@AjayiEtAl2019OpenROAD; @SkyWater2020SKY130PDK]. Because no single tool establishes every form of correctness, the report should state which properties were checked, under which assumptions, and what remains untested. **Catches:** generated code that passes a shallow check while the claim assumes hardware properties that check never tested.

- **Check 4.2: Predictive Surrogates, Tail-Ranking Fidelity, and the Optimizer's Curse.** When evaluating a surrogate that guides design-space exploration, examine its accuracy among the high-performing candidates the optimizer actually selects. Aggregate $R^2$ or root-mean-square error over millions of random unviable designs can hide large errors near the Pareto frontier. Ranking correlation (Kendall's $\tau$ or Spearman's $\rho$) within the top one to five percent of candidates is much more informative, provided the report explains how that subset was defined and what ground-truth evaluations establish its ranking. Even when overall correlation is positive, selecting top designs from noisy predictions favors candidates whose errors happen to be overly optimistic, a bias known as the optimizer's curse [@SmithWinkler2006OptimizersCurse] (@sec-law-optimizers-curse). That bias need not invert the entire ranking to exaggerate the winning candidate's benefit. Credible evidence includes reference tool evaluations of the selected candidates, their actual prediction errors and tail ranking correlation, and uncertainty estimates checked in the region reached by search. When uncertainty guides selection, explain how the search avoids chasing unsupported extrema. **Catches:** a surrogate that is accurate on average across the design space but misleading where the search converges.

- **Check 4.3: Closed-Loop Optimizers, Anti-Gaming, and Simulator Loopholes.** Closed-loop search algorithms can exploit omitted constraints in a fast simulator in the same way they exploit errors in a learned surrogate [@Strathern1997Goodhart; @AmodeiEtAl2016Concrete]. If a simulator omits DRAM refresh stalls, bypasses coherence serialization, or ignores bus wait states, an optimizer will favor configurations that lean on those shortcuts. Whenever a claim extends beyond the fast simulator itself, evaluate the winning candidate and its baseline with a check that models the suspected omission, such as cycle-accurate RTL simulation in Verilator [@Veripool2026Verilator] or field-programmable gate array (FPGA) emulation in FireSim, depending on the claim. Because switching tools proves nothing if both omit the same physical or protocol effect, identify which relevant behaviors the validation model restores and report whether the claimed gain persists, shrinks, or remains unverified under that check. **Catches:** a speedup that exists only in the evaluation simulator's blind spot.

- **Check 4.4: Multi-Objective Pareto and Constraint Integrity.** Even when the simulator or surrogate is faithful on the optimized metric, a gain along one objective can violate a boundary on another, such as thermal design power (TDP), static random-access memory (SRAM) area budget, or voltage droop. A speedup does not establish a viable architectural improvement if the candidate exceeds the chip's power or die-area limit. Different studies legitimately target different metrics: BOOM-Explorer examines power and performance tradeoffs [@BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer], whereas Ansor evaluates tensor-program execution time [@ZhengEtAl2020Ansor]. Neither objective choice means that unmeasured constraints are automatically satisfied. The evaluation should distinguish optimization objectives from hard feasibility constraints and report the full objective vectors behind its Pareto claims, together with constraint values at matched or reconciled operating points. Mark violating designs separately from the feasible frontier and state how feasibility was checked. Proxy-estimated constraints should remain labeled as estimates; an early exploration study need not provide physical signoff unless its claims require it. Record missing constraint checks separately from observed violations, keeping the scope of the claim explicit. **Catches:** a gain on the reported axis paid for by violating an unreported constraint.

## Area 5: System Orchestration, Reproducibility, and Ownership

Areas 1 through 4 examine individual problem formulations, datasets, models, and search loops. When an AI-native design system composes automated agents, deterministic compilers, and electronic design automation (EDA) tools into closed loops, three system-level questions remain: can the execution be traced and rerun, what did the full exploration cost, and who holds authority over consequential commitments such as silicon signoff? Area 5 audits execution lineage, gross resource accounting, and the boundary between automated actions and human responsibility.

- **Check 5.1: Execution Lineage, Replay, and Environment Identification.** Assess whether the execution record and released artifacts let a reviewer inspect and rerun the claimed result [@ACM2020ArtifactReview]. Because these workflows span heterogeneous toolchains (foundation-model endpoints, Python packages, simulator binaries, and synthesis scripts), small version changes can alter the outcome. Record tool and package versions, exact EDA script flags, random seeds, and model checkpoint identities with access dates. Where applicable, include container image digests (`sha256:...`) and build attestations; other environment specifications suffice when they pin the dependencies needed to rerun the work. Distinguish exact trajectory replay from repeating an experiment to check whether its scientific conclusion holds. If a checkpoint is a floating alias (`model-latest`), or seeds and script flags are undocumented, state clearly which steps cannot be reconstructed. Retained inputs, outputs, tool logs, and independent verification checks can still substantiate findings about the recorded run, while leaving repeatability open. **Catches:** a result whose execution cannot be traced, or whose reproducibility is claimed beyond what the archived artifacts support.

- **Check 5.2: Gross Cost and License Accounting.** Using that execution record, account for the total compute and economic cost of the exploration, including failed runs, timed-out simulations, and commercial EDA license hours consumed during search. Reporting only the compute of the final winning trajectory conceals the cost of the search that found it. Just as model code is only one part of a deployed learning system [@SculleyEtAl2015Hidden], inference tokens are often a fraction of a hardware workflow whose real cost lies in crashed simulations, pruned branches, and tool licenses. Rather than assuming which factor dominates, the evaluation should present a cost record covering all attempted runs (successful, failed, and timed out), setting model and token costs beside simulator compute and EDA license hours while including human effort in setup, debugging, intervention, and review. Identify any cost components that were estimated or unavailable. **Catches:** the finalist's cost reported as the search's total cost.

- **Check 5.3: Automated Actions and Human Decision Authority.** Finally, confirm that the work separates routine exploration actions delegated to automation from commitments requiring a named human authority (@sec-what-architect-owns). As @Bainbridge1983Ironies showed, automation often leaves operators with difficult monitoring and intervention tasks while stripping away the context needed to perform them; naming a human reviewer in a diagram does not by itself establish that the person can evaluate the proposed decision. While a workflow may authorize automated proposal, evaluation, and advancement within specified budgets without requiring a person to approve every step, the report should state those limits, identify which commitments require human approval, and show how exceptions reach the responsible architect. Whenever a commitment involves verification signoff or silicon fabrication, the workflow must surface the tradeoffs and residual verification gaps clearly enough that the person signing off knows what risk is being accepted. **Catches:** a system that has quietly acquired authority beyond its assigned limits.

## Required Content of a Complete-Workflow Report

A reviewer can apply the seventeen items in Areas 1 through 5 individually when a paper evaluates a single component, such as a learned cost model, a placement policy, or an RTL generator. When a study instead claims a complete human-plus-technical design workflow, it must also explain how those item-level findings fit together on the same tasks, baselines, and claims. The six parts in @tbl-complete-system-assessment provide a reading order for that synthesis: the system configuration and comparator establish what was tested, the architecture result establishes what the hardware achieved, and controlled component ablations alongside cost and reliability records help explain why. Keeping those layers distinct matters because an individual component can make a measurable contribution even when the complete workflow fails to beat a strong practical alternative, and an overall workflow gain does not prove that every component inside it helped. The closing statement of claims must preserve both distinctions alongside the limits of the evidence.

| **Part of the report** | **Required content** |
| --- | --- |
| **System identity and comparator** | The configured system, the complete workflow, the architectural task, the environment, the legal actions, the hardware checks, the budgets, and the strongest practical alternative. State what was fixed before the runs, what changed during exploration, and which configuration produced each reported result. Check 1.2 addresses comparison budgets; explain which resources were matched and how remaining differences affect the comparison. |
| **Architecture result** | For each hardware task, the supported result or the failure, the comparator it was measured against, its uncertainty, the deepest check that completed, and the nonclaims stated outright. Manufacturing, test, packaging, or bring-up evidence appears only when the evaluation reached those stages. Check 4.1 addresses correctness and implementation evidence; this part asks where each task's evidence stops and whether it reaches the level needed for the claim. |
| **Decision behavior and component contribution** | Useful observations, supported decisions, false accepts and false rejects, escalations, stops, recoveries, and human overrides, reported where applicable as counts a reader can audit. State how decision errors were established and identify cases whose correctness remains unknown. Separate the complete-workflow effect from each claimed component contribution through a controlled comparison that removes or replaces that component; where such a comparison is absent, leave the contribution unattributed. |
| **Total cost and candidate flow** | Resource classes, per-run design costs, and the candidate flow of every comparison arm from proposal to acceptance or rejection, with failed and censored work retained and shared costs accounted for without double counting. Check 5.2 already asks for the cost record; this part asks that the flow of candidates through it be visible per arm. |
| **Reliability, benchmark, and challenge results** | Repeated behavior across seeds and reruns where relevant, the envelope of conditions tested, the versions and health of every benchmark used, and red-team and fault-injection results where relevant to the claim. Name untested conditions and structural attacks that limit the conclusions. Checks 3.1 and 4.3 already ask for benchmark health and simulator loopholes; this part connects their coverage and remaining gaps to the workflow's reliability claims. |
| **Claim status** | The complete-workflow claim and each narrower component claim stated separately, with the tasks, conditions, costs, architectural checks, and challenge coverage within which each is asserted, and a plain statement of which of them the evidence supports, which it does not, and which it leaves undecided. |
: **The final report connects the evidence to the claims rather than repeating it.** Six parts in reading order, from the system and comparison through architecture result, decision behavior, cost, and reliability to the claim status. A part that overlaps a checklist item points back to that evidence and explains what it establishes for the workflow. {#tbl-complete-system-assessment tbl-colwidths="[26,74]"}

The final row of @tbl-complete-system-assessment asks authors to state their complete-workflow and component claims, together with the scope of each, in their own words. It requires neither a specialized record format nor the formal program-claim verdicts defined in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect, because the item findings recorded across Areas 1 through 5 already supply the evidence for judging those claims. What matters is making the scope explicit: missing evidence leaves a claim undecided, observed failures contradict it or narrow its valid domain, and without a plain closing statement even thorough item-level evidence leaves the reader to guess what the workflow actually established.

## Findings Summary

Whether a review evaluates a standalone method or a complete workflow, @tbl-ai-arch-evaluation-matrix gathers the five checklist areas onto a single page: what each area protects, what evidence supports a claim, and which gaps or failures call a conclusion into question. Because evidence requirements always follow the scope of the claim, the review records what was checked, what was found, and how those findings bound the paper's conclusions, distinguishing missing evidence from demonstrated failure and noting whenever a check does not apply.

| **Area** | **What it protects** | **Evidence that could support the claim** | **Examples of gaps or failures to investigate** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1: System Framing and Scope** | The method suits the problem and the comparison is fair | Comparisons with relevant classical heuristics and analytical models; ablations of claimed contributions; baselines under comparable resource constraints, with differences explained; end-to-end effort accounting | Learning used where a closed-form solution exists without explaining its benefit; a starved baseline; the Amdahl consequence unexamined |
| **2: Data Representations** | The representation can express the property the claim is about | Evidence that required structure is preserved; legalization results and measured post-legalization degradation where relevant; cross-fidelity ranking checks at the levels needed by the claim | Flattening that loses required hierarchy; unroutable decoded output where routability is claimed; a frontier that inverts at synthesis |
| **3: Data Integrity and Leakage** | The claimed gain is assessed against contamination and leakage risks, and generalization is bounded | Disclosure of contamination checks and their limits; split isolation suited to the task, including temporal or block-level separation where relevant; a stated validity envelope | Evidence of benchmark memorization; normalization computed over the test set; extrapolation beyond the evaluated conditions without supporting evidence |
| **4: Learning Methods and Proxies** | Correctness and proxy fidelity are checked where candidates are generated or selected | Checks appropriate to the artifact and claim, potentially including static timing analysis (STA), clock-domain crossing (CDC) analysis, design rule check (DRC), and layout versus schematic (LVS); selected-candidate error and top-$k$ rank correlation; independent checks for proxy gaming; Pareto vectors covering the claimed objectives and constraints | Compilation-only evidence for functional correctness; aggregate accuracy that hides error among selected candidates; a gain that vanishes in cycle-accurate simulation; a violated unreported constraint |
| **5: System Orchestration** | Reproduction limits, total cost, and responsibility for decisions are explicit | Execution history and sufficient environment, tool, and model details for the stated reproduction scope, using pinned image digests and checkpoints where available; total cost accounting covering failed runs; explicit automated and human action rights and responsibility | Floating model endpoints with uncharacterized effects on repeatability; finalist-only cost; automated commitment authority without defined limits or accountable ownership |
: **Findings summary for the five checklist areas.** Each row names what the area protects, evidence that could support the relevant claim, and examples of gaps or failures to investigate. {#tbl-ai-arch-evaluation-matrix tbl-colwidths="[18,24,30,28]"}

Taken together, the five areas help reviewers determine whether apparent architectural progress is supported by evidence rather than explained by unmatched compute scale, benchmark recall, or simulator and surrogate error. The resulting findings state plainly what the evidence supports, what remains uncertain, and how each gap or observed failure limits the claim. Forming an acceptance or signoff recommendation requires a separate human judgment; the checklist stops at the findings.
